scenes.tts: Why would a cell surrounded by cholesterol keep making more? Brown and Goldstein saw this in skin cells from children with familial hypercholesterolemia. L D L crowded the medium, yet the cells behaved as though cholesterol were scarce.
scenes.caption: Why would a cell surrounded by cholesterol keep making more? Brown and Goldstein saw this in skin cells from children with familial hypercholesterolemia. LDL crowded the medium, yet the cells behaved as though cholesterol were scarce.
scenes.visual: Hook first, with no title. Draw one large schematic skin-cell cross-section filling about two-thirds of the frame. Along its left edge, a channel labelled 'LDL in medium' carries many bright LDL circles past the membrane. Inside, a small cholesterol-production conveyor keeps sending gold tokens toward an ER ribbon. Reveal the question only after the crowded channel and running conveyor are visible. Keep the LDL circles drifting and the conveyor belt rolling throughout all three sentences; draw no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Why would a cell surrounded by cholesterol keep making more? Brown and Goldstein saw this in skin cells from children with familial hypercholesterolemia. LDL crowded the medium, yet the cells behaved as though cholesterol were scarce.

scenes.visual: Keep the same moving cell world. Dim it slightly while 'THE CHOLESTEROL GAUGE' writes across the middle, then clear the title. LDL circles continue drifting behind the letters, and the internal conveyor continues rolling, so this two-second card never freezes.

scenes.tts: A liver cell gets cholesterol through two supply lines. It can build cholesterol, or pull L D L from blood through L D L receptors. But the cell does not measure L D L outside. It measures cholesterol reaching its endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
scenes.caption: A liver cell gets cholesterol through two supply lines. It can build cholesterol, or pull LDL from blood through LDL receptors. But the cell does not measure LDL outside. It measures cholesterol reaching its endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
scenes.visual: Transform the existing cell label from 'skin cell' to 'liver cell' and widen the left channel into blood. As 'two supply lines' is spoken, grow two thick routes into the same ER cholesterol gauge: an upper route from an LDL receptor at the surface and a lower route from a box labelled 'build'. Send gold tokens along both routes. When the narration contrasts outside with the ER, let several LDL circles pass the surface without changing the gauge, then send one internal gold token into the gauge and move its needle. The two token streams keep moving throughout.
scenes.narration: A liver cell gets cholesterol through two supply lines. It can build cholesterol, or pull LDL from blood through LDL receptors. But the cell does not measure LDL outside. It measures cholesterol reaching its endoplasmic reticulum membrane.

scenes.tts: On the import line, an L D L receptor captures L D L at the cell surface. The particle enters, and its cholesterol joins the cell's internal pool. A working receptor changes what the gauge can see.
scenes.caption: On the import line, an LDL receptor captures LDL at the cell surface. The particle enters, and its cholesterol joins the cell's internal pool. A working receptor changes what the gauge can see.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the upper route without leaving the cell cross-section. Use two membrane bars, one labelled receptor cup, and one LDL circle; mark the whole drawing 'schematic'. The cup catches the moving circle, carries it inside, and releases a gold cholesterol token. The token travels toward the ER pool and nudges the gauge upward. Repeat a slower capture in the background while the last sentence lands; no atom-by-atom or bond drawing.
scenes.narration: On the import line, an LDL receptor captures LDL at the cell surface. The particle enters, and its cholesterol joins the cell's internal pool. A working receptor changes what the gauge can see.

scenes.tts: On the synthesis line, acetyl coenzyme A feeds the long road toward cholesterol. The main throttle, though not the only one, is H M G coenzyme A reductase. It makes mevalonate in a rate-limiting, irreversible step, and statins inhibit it.
scenes.caption: On the synthesis line, acetyl-CoA feeds the long road toward cholesterol. The main throttle, though not the only one, is HMG-CoA reductase. It makes mevalonate in a rate-limiting, irreversible step, and statins inhibit it.
scenes.visual: Pan down to the lower route in the same liver cell. Draw a wide pipe labelled 'schematic' carrying small blocks labelled 'acetyl-CoA' that turn into blocks labelled 'HMG-CoA' just before a large valve labelled 'HMG-CoA reductase' (the valve takes HMG-CoA, not acetyl-CoA). As the enzyme is named, the valve turns and a block labelled 'mevalonate' emerges, followed by moving gold tokens heading toward the ER pool. On 'statins inhibit it', slide a red statin stop into the valve and slow the stream to a trickle while the upstream blocks continue to queue.
scenes.narration: On the synthesis line, acetyl-CoA feeds the long road toward cholesterol. The main throttle, though not the only one, is HMG-CoA reductase. It makes mevalonate in a rate-limiting, irreversible step, and statins inhibit it.

scenes.tts: One E R cholesterol gauge sets both synthesis and L D L uptake. S C A P is the sensor, and S R E B P two is the passenger. When cholesterol binds S C A P, Insig grips S C A P. The complex stays in the E R.
scenes.caption: One ER cholesterol gauge sets both synthesis and LDL uptake. SCAP is the sensor, and SREBP-2 is the passenger. When cholesterol binds SCAP, Insig grips SCAP. The complex stays in the ER.
scenes.visual: Bring the ER ribbon and its gauge to the center, still connected to both supply routes. Represent SCAP as a labelled sensor cart embedded in the ER and SREBP-2 as a labelled passenger attached to it; these are cartoons, not protein structures. A gold cholesterol token docks on SCAP, then a clasp labelled 'Insig' slides over SCAP. The cart tries to move toward a small Golgi stack but the clasp holds it at the ER. ER lipids drift gently and the gauge needle quivers while the complex is held.
scenes.narration: One ER cholesterol gauge sets both synthesis and LDL uptake. SCAP is the sensor, and SREBP-2 is the passenger. When cholesterol binds SCAP, Insig grips SCAP. The complex stays in the ER.

scenes.tts: When E R cholesterol falls, S C A P escapes Insig. It carries S R E B P two to the Golgi, where enzymes release its active piece. That piece enters the nucleus. It raises both H M G coenzyme A reductase and the L D L receptor.
scenes.caption: When ER cholesterol falls, SCAP escapes Insig. It carries SREBP-2 to the Golgi, where enzymes release its active piece. That piece enters the nucleus. It raises both HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor.
scenes.visual: Drain gold tokens from the ER gauge and let its needle fall. The Insig clasp opens; the same SCAP cart carries its SREBP-2 passenger along a dotted route to the Golgi. There, split off one small piece labelled 'active SREBP-2' and move it into the nucleus. From the nucleus, grow two arrows back into the carried world: one increases the count of reductase valves, and the other increases receptor cups at the surface. Keep the dotted route flowing until both counters finish rising.
scenes.narration: When ER cholesterol falls, SCAP escapes Insig. It carries SREBP-2 to the Golgi, where enzymes release its active piece. That piece enters the nucleus. It raises both HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor.

scenes.tts: Predict the statin's indirect effect. If synthesis falls, what happens to L D L receptor number? Fewer, more, or unchanged?
scenes.caption: Predict the statin's indirect effect. If synthesis falls, what happens to LDL receptor number? Fewer, more, or unchanged?
scenes.visual: Return to the full liver-cell cross-section. The red statin stop closes the synthesis valve and the ER gauge begins falling. Above the surface receptors, place a large question mark and three compact choices: 'fewer', 'more', 'unchanged'. Keep gold tokens draining slowly from the ER and the gauge needle descending during the question. Do not reveal a choice.
scenes.narration: Predict the statin's indirect effect. If synthesis falls, what happens to LDL receptor number? Fewer, more, or unchanged?

scenes.visual: Hold the same prediction and all three choices for four and a half seconds. This is the deliberate thinking pause. Let the ER gauge needle continue a very slow descent, pulse the question mark once, and drift LDL circles through the blood channel; reveal no answer.

scenes.tts: A statin lowers cholesterol production, so the E R gauge reads low. S R E B P two then turns up the L D L receptor gene. More receptors pull more L D L from blood. The drug closes the making line, and the gauge opens the import line.
scenes.caption: A statin lowers cholesterol production, so the ER gauge reads low. SREBP-2 then turns up the LDL-receptor gene. More receptors pull more LDL from blood. The drug closes the making line, and the gauge opens the import line.
scenes.visual: Highlight 'more' and transform the single surface receptor into a row of receptor cups. Show active SREBP-2 moving into the nucleus again, then animate the receptor counter rising. Increase the rate at which LDL circles leave the blood and enter the cell; a small blood-LDL meter falls. Keep the lower synthesis valve visibly blocked while the upper import stream accelerates, making the two-line tradeoff visible throughout.
scenes.narration: A statin lowers cholesterol production, so the ER gauge reads low. SREBP-2 then turns up the LDL-receptor gene. More receptors pull more LDL from blood. The drug closes the making line, and the gauge opens the import line.

scenes.tts: Familial hypercholesterolemia reveals the same logic from the opposite direction. With too few working receptors, little L D L cholesterol gets inside. In the dish, the skin cells' E R gauge stayed low, so synthesis kept running. In the body, blood L D L rises mainly because clearance is slow.
scenes.caption: Familial hypercholesterolemia reveals the same logic from the opposite direction. With too few working receptors, little LDL cholesterol gets inside. In the dish, the skin cells' ER gauge stayed low, so synthesis kept running. In the body, blood LDL rises mainly because clearance is slow.
scenes.visual: Remove most receptor cups and place a small 'FH' tag beside the remaining nonworking cup. LDL circles now pass without entering and accumulate in the blood channel; its LDL meter climbs. Remove the statin stop. On 'In the dish', transform the cell label back to 'skin cell'; because few gold tokens reach the ER, hold the gauge low and restart the synthesis conveyor. On 'In the body', relabel it 'liver cell' and let the blood LDL meter keep climbing while the conveyor runs at its ordinary pace, not faster (the lesson says the FH liver does not make much more). Keep the outside pile circulating and the inside conveyor moving in opposite directions to resolve the opening puzzle.
scenes.narration: Familial hypercholesterolemia reveals the same logic from the opposite direction. With too few working receptors, little LDL cholesterol gets inside. In the dish, the skin cells' ER gauge stayed low, so synthesis kept running. In the body, blood LDL rises mainly because clearance is slow.

scenes.tts: Follow cholesterol into the E R, and the puzzle dissolves. A cell responds to cholesterol it can sense, not cholesterol merely nearby. Low E R cholesterol turns up both making and importing.
scenes.caption: Follow cholesterol into the ER, and the puzzle dissolves. A cell responds to cholesterol it can sense, not cholesterol merely nearby. Low ER cholesterol turns up both making and importing.
scenes.visual: Replay the whole idea as one continuous movement in the carried cell. Track one LDL circle from blood through a receptor, then track its gold cholesterol token into the ER gauge. Briefly let the gauge rise and both supply arrows thin. On the final sentence, reverse to a low gauge and thicken both the synthesis and import arrows together. End with both moving arrows framing the ER gauge; do not introduce any new label.
scenes.narration: Follow cholesterol into the ER, and the puzzle dissolves. A cell responds to cholesterol it can sense, not cholesterol merely nearby. Low ER cholesterol turns up both making and importing.

scenes.visual: House end card. Over a faint silhouette of the same ER gauge and two slowly moving supply arrows, show the exact line 'Low ER cholesterol turns up both making and importing.' Hex waves once beneath it. Keep every element inside the safe frame; the line is nine words and remains the dominant object.
